sources_considered.why: A controlled experiment distinguishes voice and grammatical-person effects.
Controlled Turing tests establish human identification errors, with a different outcome from beliefs about internal processes.
Humanlike tone and social-perception correlations do not establish the claimed causal effect on beliefs about cognition.

evidence_items.explanation: The experiment found greater anthropomorphism with speech plus text, but no grammatical-person effect. It supports a role for presentation cues while limiting the inference that humanlike wording itself explains the claimed belief.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv; Cameron R. Jones and Benjamin K. Bergen
evidence_items.explanation: Participants often selected the persona-prompted model as the human conversational partner. This establishes successful imitation in the test, but does not measure whether people who know they are using an LLM believe it has humanlike internal processes.

unresolved_gaps: No retrieved study jointly establishes the specified language mechanism, recurring attribution of humanlike cognitive processes, and the mistaken nature of that attribution.
The experiments measure different outcomes: general anthropomorphism and human-versus-machine identification.
The evidence does not establish a general-population frequency for the claimed effect.
